ai_peak.text: This metric suggests AI is still in the acceleration phase, roughly 340 days before a potential peak. Caveat: analogies to past bubbles often break down due to structural differences in technology, capital, and market dynamics.

buffett.text: Market cap to GDP suggests AI valuations are following the dot-com trajectory but at an accelerated pace, currently at late-1998 intensity levels. A skeptical reader should note that analogies based on single metrics can mislead, since AI companies have real revenue streams unlike many dot-com firms.

capex.text: AI infrastructure spending is rising steeply and matches dot-com's acceleration phase, suggesting sustained investment appetite. However, AI capex may reflect genuine long-term utility rather than speculative excess, making spending intensity alone a poor crash predictor.

ipo_froth.text: IPO enthusiasm shows similar early-stage dynamics to the dot-com boom, with first-day pops still modest relative to peak froth. The pattern suggests room for further euphoria before any potential reversal. Caveat: IPO metrics lag actual market peaks, so this analogy may understate how far sentiment has already advanced.

it_invest.text:
IT investment share has followed the dot-com arc so far, with AI spending climbing steeply but still shy of peak bubble intensity. The analogy suggests continued acceleration, though investment patterns may compress differently given today's capital efficiency and market structure.

Caveat: Historical analogies work until they don't, and AI's underlying productivity case remains genuinely contested.

margin_debt.text: Margin debt has roughly doubled since ChatGPT, reaching 41% of dot-com peak intensity. The pattern of rising leverage mirrors the late-1990s acceleration phase, suggesting investors are increasingly confident or complacent. Keep in mind that regulatory changes and circuit breakers since 2000 may prevent debt from reaching comparable extremes.

market_concentration.text: AI market concentration is rising steeply but remains well below dot-com extremes, suggesting earlier bubble stages. The compression ratio implies a faster timeline, but concentration alone cannot predict peaks, only describe current structure.

monetary.text: Monetary and sentiment conditions today show fundamentally different patterns than the dot-com era, suggesting any timeline based on this metric is unreliable. Skeptics should note that AI's actual funding sources and market psychology may simply follow different rules than 1990s tech stocks did.

nasdaq.text: The Nasdaq has risen 2.4x since ChatGPT, matching where the dot-com bubble stood roughly 11 months before its peak. This suggests the AI rally could have years to run if the analogy holds, though past bubbles don't always follow identical trajectories and sector composition matters enormously.

price_appreciation.text: AI valuations are rising sharply but remain below dot-com peak intensity, suggesting either sustained growth ahead or room for further acceleration before any reversal. Caveat: price momentum alone says nothing about whether underlying fundamentals justify these valuations.

semis.text: Semiconductor production lacks a clear peak phase in the dot-com era, making this metric unsuitable for drawing parallels. Skeptics should remember that chip demand has structural drivers today that didn't exist then, potentially invalidating any historical comparison.

sentiment.text: Consumer sentiment shows no signs of following the dot-com pattern. While the dot-com era saw sentiment surge toward its peak, current sentiment remains flat or declining, suggesting a fundamentally different market psychology between these booms. Skeptics should note that sentiment measures can reflect lagging rather than leading indicators of market stress.

sp500.text: The S&P 500 has risen 1.9x since ChatGPT, reaching about 63% of dot-com peak intensity, suggesting the AI boom may have further to run before any potential reversal. The analogy points to a peak around early 2028, though this assumes current acceleration continues at a comparable pace. Caveat: market dynamics have changed significantly since 2000, and the AI boom's economic fundamentals differ from dot-com's.

speculation.text: Speculative fervor in AI is building at a pace slightly faster than the dot-com run-up, currently at about one-third the intensity seen at that market's peak. The caveat: past compression ratios offer no guarantee about when or whether AI speculation will actually peak.

tech_leadership.text: Tech leadership concentration has risen sharply since ChatGPT, tracking the dot-com pattern at a compressed pace. The analogy suggests a potential peak around late 2026, though this assumes structural similarities that may not hold. Caveat: the metric measures leadership only, not whether the underlying AI investments prove economically valuable.

tech_orders.text: Tech equipment orders show AI following the dot-com trajectory, currently at 76% of dot-com peak intensity and accelerating. The analogy suggests similar boom dynamics, though the comparison relies on historical data quality that may not fully capture structural differences between the two eras.

valuation.text: AI valuations are climbing steeply but haven't yet matched dot-com excess, suggesting the boom may have further to run before any reversal. Caveat: valuation alone cannot predict peaks, since market psychology and external shocks matter as much as fundamentals.

valuation_multiple.text: Stock valuations are rising as steeply in AI's boom as they did before the dot-com crash, and we're currently at roughly 89% of peak intensity. Skeptics should remember that valuation multiples alone cannot predict crashes—market peaks depend on earnings growth, sentiment shifts, and dozens of other factors that may play out very differently this time.

yield_curve.text: The yield curve shows no signs of mimicking the dot-com era's pattern, remaining flat while the comparable dot-com period was already steepening toward its peak. This suggests financial conditions differ fundamentally between the two booms. Caveat: yield curve dynamics depend heavily on Federal Reserve policy, which operates under different constraints and philosophies than in 2000.
